lessons.title: Files, Programs, Processes, and the Terminal
lessons.summary: A source file is data; a program is executable instructions; a process is a running instance with memory and operating-system resources.
lessons.body:
Files, Programs, Processes, and the Terminal

Why this matters
A source file is data; a program is executable instructions; a process is a running instance with memory and operating-system resources. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• A source file is data; a program is executable instructions; a process is a running instance with memory and operating-system resources.
• The terminal is a text interface to the operating system. The shell parses commands, resolves executables through PATH, sets environment variables, and starts processes.
• The working directory changes how relative paths resolve. Many 'file not found' errors are simply the right command from the wrong directory.
• Ports identify network endpoints owned by processes. localhost means the current machine, not 'the frontend'.

Step-by-step walkthrough
1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level.
2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise.
3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment.
4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes.
5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic.
6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill.

TaskFlow connection
Later in the course, how the web and development environment work stops being an isolated topic and becomes infrastructure for real features. When you encounter files, programs, processes, and the terminal again, ask which layer owns it, what its inputs are, what output proves success, and what failure evidence is available. That prevents you from copying framework snippets without understanding the underlying browser, runtime, operating-system, or language behavior.

Guided exercise
Create a tiny example from scratch without copying the final code from a tutorial. Keep the example under about 30–50 lines where possible. After it works, deliberately break one assumption. Write the exact symptom and the smallest fix. Then delete the experiment or commit it in a dedicated practice folder so it does not pollute production project structure.

Check your understanding
• Can you describe the concept without naming a framework?
• Can you point to the exact input and output?
• Can you name one common incorrect assumption?
• Can you reproduce the idea in a tiny example?
• Can you diagnose one intentional failure using evidence rather than guesses?

Instructor note
Do not rush because the syntax looks easy. Most difficult full-stack bugs are not caused by forgetting syntax; they come from an incorrect model of ownership, execution environment, identity, time, or data flow. The foundation track exists so later lessons can move quickly without becoming mysterious.

Browser, Server, HTTP Request, and Response

lessons.title: JavaScript Runtime: Browser vs Node.js
lessons.summary: JavaScript is a language; browser and Node.js are runtimes that provide different host APIs.
lessons.body:
JavaScript Runtime: Browser vs Node.js

Why this matters
JavaScript is a language; browser and Node.js are runtimes that provide different host APIs. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. • JavaScript is a language; browser and Node.js are runtimes that provide different host APIs.

This lab converts the previous explanation into a small piece of evidence you created yourself. Do not begin by copying the finished example. Start with the behavior you expect, then make the computer prove or disprove your model.

Your task
Launch a small local server, discover its PID/port from another terminal, stop it cleanly, then reproduce an address-in-use error.

Working method
1. Create the smallest clean starting point.
2. Predict the first result in writing.
3. Implement only enough to test that prediction.
4. Run it and capture the result.
5. Add one intentional failure or changed assumption.
6. Diagnose from evidence before editing randomly.
7. Restore the correct behavior.
8. Close the reference and reproduce the important part from memory.

Why this is separate from the concept lesson
Reading can create familiarity without recall. The separate lab forces retrieval, execution, and debugging. Those three abilities are what later framework lessons assume when the codebase becomes larger.

You have a runnable example, one recorded prediction, one successful result, one controlled failure with diagnosis, and a short explain-back in your own words.

lessons.title: A Professional Debugging Method
lessons.summary: Reproduce first; do not modify code while the symptom is still vague.
lessons.body:
A Professional Debugging Method

Why this matters
Reproduce first; do not modify code while the symptom is still vague. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Reproduce first; do not modify code while the symptom is still vague.
• Observe exact evidence: command output, stack trace, request/response, logs, state, or database rows.
• Form one hypothesis and change one variable so cause and effect remain visible.
• Write the root cause in plain language after the fix; the explanation proves more learning than memorizing the command.

Step-by-step walkthrough
1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level.
2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise.
3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment.
4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes.
5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic.
6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill.

TaskFlow connection
Later in the course, how the web and development environment work stops being an isolated topic and becomes infrastructure for real features. When you encounter a professional debugging method again, ask which layer owns it, what its inputs are, what output proves success, and what failure evidence is available. That prevents you from copying framework snippets without understanding the underlying browser, runtime, operating-system, or language behavior.

Guided exercise
Create a tiny example from scratch without copying the final code from a tutorial. Keep the example under about 30–50 lines where possible. After it works, deliberately break one assumption. Write the exact symptom and the smallest fix. Then delete the experiment or commit it in a dedicated practice folder so it does not pollute production project structure.

Check your understanding
• Can you describe the concept without naming a framework?
• Can you point to the exact input and output?
• Can you name one common incorrect assumption?
• Can you reproduce the idea in a tiny example?
• Can you diagnose one intentional failure using evidence rather than guesses?

Instructor note
Do not rush because the syntax looks easy. Most difficult full-stack bugs are not caused by forgetting syntax; they come from an incorrect model of ownership, execution environment, identity, time, or data flow. The foundation track exists so later lessons can move quickly without becoming mysterious.
